statement: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. A later narrative review (Faria et al., 2020; second-hand, PubMed searched to October 2019 with one author mainly responsible) has 52 table rows about phenethylamine-associated cases,50 labelled MDMA, and 21 outcomes labelled death. The 36 rows with sodium have lowest values 101–130 mmol/L; one of those rows also reports an earlier value 137, not an extra case. Two patients appear twice; one case cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper; three fatal rows record no low sodium; and one outcome is blank despite a death in the cited title. The authorless 2001 case is traceable, while another row's compound label conflicts with its reference title. Ten fatal rows come from the California series, so the review must not be added to it as an independent 52-person series. Amounts are unknown or blank in 30 rows, including 14 of 21 fatal rows. The review's single-dose statement is restricted to most reported deaths or permanent neurological injuries in women aged 15–30; its table cannot verify that statement. In the 10 fatal rows with sodium, values 109–126 mmol/L lie within the 101–130 range in the 24 recovery rows with sodium (editors' counts). The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. Faria also proposes sodium loss in sweat, while describing the drinking reports as anecdotal and the mechanisms as not fully understood. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, and the 2020 review cites no study that measured how much people drank, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017).
plain: After MDMA, some young people have been treated in hospital because the salt (sodium) in their blood fell too low, causing fits and swelling of the brain. It started within hours of taking MDMA. In a UK group of 17 people aged 15 to 26, at least 10 had drunk a lot of fluid, and two died: both had taken one tablet, had been drinking a lot of water, and drank or were given more water after they felt ill. In California, 73 of 188 people who had their sodium measured had a low level, and 4 of them died. These are reports of people who became ill, so they cannot show how often it happens. Most of the UK group had taken one or two tablets, and no study has compared amounts. The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water; that part is not proven.

risk_of_bias.note: Both series are ROBINS-I critical on their cards: cases are those that were reported to a poison service, exposure is by history (MDMA confirmed in only part), sodium was recorded in about a third of the Californian cases, and values were given by telephone. One level, not two, because the claim describes what was seen in these cases and gives no rate.

inconsistency.note: The UK and Californian series, from different countries, years and services, agree on the pattern (young people, within hours, seizures and brain swelling). They differ in the share of women (10 of 17 against 55 of 73 low-sodium cases), which the claim leaves to the separate claim on who is affected.

indirectness.note: Worded for people who came to a poison service or hospital, with the limits stated.

imprecision.note: Small counts (2 deaths in 17; 4 in 73), no intervals for any share, and an internal inconsistency in the Californian count of low-sodium cases (73 and 74).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the published case reports are selected by nature, and the claim takes no figure from them.

grade.reasoning: Case series start low (observational, no comparison group for the UK series). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3). The claim states what was recorded in two poison-service series and, as described in a narrative review, in published case reports, and that none could give a rate. Status replicated: two independent services in two countries show the same pattern; the 2008 review adds nothing independent, because its table draws on the California series and appears to include a UK case that is also in the first series, and the 2020 review (Faria et al.) is not an independent 52-person cohort: its table draws 10 of its 21 labelled deaths from the California series and contains errors (card sc_faria_2020), so it is cited for what it tabulates, with the errors stated. The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and as untested here; it is not part of what the claim asserts. No advice on fluid or on amounts is given.

statement: Among people reported to California poison control in 2000 to 2005 with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded blood sodium (188 of 545 cases; Rosenson et al., 2007), low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) was found in 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), an odds ratio of 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59), which is 31 more in 100 women than men among those tested (editors' calculation); sodium was recorded about as often in women (35 in 100) as in men (33 in 100). Within each sex, women with low sodium had higher odds of coma (odds ratio 3.93, 1.20 to 12.90) and of seizure (4.38, 1.74 to 11.00) than women without it, while in men the intervals for coma (0.78, 0.15 to 3.97) and seizure (2.21, 0.69 to 7.07) included 1. These are counts of people who became ill and were reported, not rates in people who take MDMA: sodium was recorded in only 35 in 100 of the cases, and the authors say that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and differences between individuals prevent determining causality. The paper gives neither the amount of fluid drunk nor the amount of MDMA taken. The only comparison read of women and men given the same amount is described second-hand in a 2020 narrative review (Faria et al., 2020): in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study, 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women were given 125 mg of MDMA (study condition; the review does not specify the setting), and copeptin, a marker of the water-holding hormone, rose in the women but not in the men, while no significant differences were reported in the hormone itself or in blood sodium; the review does not identify that statistical contrast, so it cannot be treated as a demonstrated absence of a sex difference. The direction is the same, without a test, in the UK series in which 10 of 17 patients and both who died were female (Hartung et al., 2002), in an earlier series of 18 cases with 17 women that the California paper cites and that was not read, and, as described in a narrative review (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand), in more than 85 in 100 of published symptomatic cases, whose table draws 10 rows from the California series and so is not independent; the 2020 review's table of published cases (1991 to 2018) lists 46 female rows among 52 (88.5 in 100 by editorial calculation, whereas the review prints 89 in 100), from which it infers that women are predisposed, but the table appears to count two patients twice (conditionally 44 of 50, 88 in 100, editors' calculation, not a verified unique-patient count), cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one woman's case, draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series and sets no case count against the number of women and men who take MDMA. These series are of young people (mean age 21 in California; 15 to 26 in the UK series), so age cannot be compared. Reasons the authors and the reviews offer (metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen effects on water retention and on the brain's response to low sodium; lower muscle mass and body weight) were not tested in people who took MDMA; the 2020 review's main support for a greater risk to women once the brain swells comes from patients after surgery, among whom women who still menstruated were about 25 times more likely than men or women past menopause to die or have lasting brain injury (Ayus et al., 1992, as described in the review).
plain: In California poison-centre records, women with MDMA illness were more likely than men to have a low level of blood sodium: 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) against 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), among those who had their sodium measured. Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma. The reports count people who became ill and were reported, not everyone who took MDMA, and sodium was measured in about a third of them, so this does not show how likely low sodium is in women or men who take MDMA. A review describes one small controlled study in 8 women and 8 men. A marker of the water-holding hormone rose only in the women; no clear differences in the hormone itself or in sodium were reported, but the review does not say which comparison that refers to. These were mostly young people (average age 21).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical on the card: the people are those who were reported and tested (spectrum and referral bias), sodium was recorded in about a third, the odds ratios are unadjusted for body weight, amount of MDMA, fluid intake or other drugs, and exposure is by history.

inconsistency.note: The UK series and the two reviews' case tables point the same way, though they are descriptions without a test and the tables overlap the California series. The small controlled crossover, described second-hand, reports no significant hormone/sodium differences without identifying the contrast; it concerns selected healthy volunteers under fixed study conditions, not on who was found among reported cases, so it qualifies the claim rather than contradicting it.

indirectness.note: Worded for people who became ill and were reported, which is what was studied.

imprecision.note: The main interval (2.08 to 7.59) excludes 1 but is wide; the within-sex odds ratios for coma and seizure have intervals up to 12.90 and 7.07.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the odds ratio (about 4) is large, but the people studied are those reported and tested, and unmeasured differences in body weight, amount taken and fluid drunk could produce or hide it (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: One poison-centre case series with a comparison inside it starts low (observational). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Relation: is associated with; the authors themselves say causality cannot be determined, and sex is bound up with body size, amount taken and fluid drunk, none of which was recorded. Status single study: only the California series tests the sex difference among reported cases; the UK series and the two reviews are consistent but do not test it, and both reviews' tables overlap the California series. The 2020 review (Faria et al.; card sc_faria_2020) infers a female predisposition from its case counts, but its table has errors and no denominators, and the only controlled comparison it describes (Simmler et al., 2011, not read) reports no significant hormone/sodium differences without identifying the statistical contrast; that study and the postoperative data (Ayus et al., 1992, not read) are second-hand. The answer to who is most at risk cannot be read from this claim: it gives who was found among reported cases with a sodium result, not who is at risk among people who take MDMA, and no age comparison is possible.
